Ecclesiastes 1.audience: Ecclesiastes presents the words of "the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem" (Ecclesiastes 1:1). The Hebrew title, Qoheleth, means one who gathers an assembly.

culture.title: Vanity
culture.text: The Hebrew word translated "vanity" means vapor or breath—something fleeting. It appears over thirty times in the book.

culture.title: Under the sun
culture.text: "Under the sun" appears about thirty times, describing life in this world.

culture.title: Rivers to the sea
culture.text: "All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full"—an observation of the water cycle.

Ecclesiastes 2.audience: The Preacher describes testing pleasure, building, wealth, and work, in terms that fit a wealthy king's life.

culture.title: Gardens and pools
culture.text: Kings built gardens, orchards, and pools to water them. Royal parks were a mark of wealth in Persia and earlier empires.

culture.title: Singers and instruments
culture.text: Royal courts kept male and female singers for entertainment (2 Samuel 19:35).

Ecclesiastes 3.audience: The poem "To every thing there is a season" (Ecclesiastes 3:1) lists fourteen pairs of opposite times. It is often read at funerals today.

culture.title: Casting away stones
culture.text: Farmers cleared stones from fields before planting, and gathered stones for walls and buildings.

culture.title: Rending and sewing
culture.text: Clothes were torn in grief and mended afterward.

Ecclesiastes 4.audience: The Preacher observes oppression, envy, and the loneliness of a man who works without companion or heir.

culture.title: Two are better than one
culture.text: Travelers alone could freeze at night or be attacked. Companions helped each other up, kept each other warm, and defended each other.

culture.title: A threefold cord
culture.text: Rope was made by twisting strands together; three strands are much stronger than one.

Ecclesiastes 5.audience: The Preacher gives advice on worship—listening rather than rash vows—and on the emptiness of hoarded wealth.

culture.title: Paying vows
culture.text: Vows made to God had to be paid (Deuteronomy 23:21). It is better not to vow than to vow and fail to pay.

culture.title: Layers of officials
culture.text: "He that is higher than the highest regardeth; and there be higher than they"—officials watching officials in a large government.

Ecclesiastes 6.audience: The Preacher describes a man with wealth, many children, and long life who still cannot enjoy what he has.

culture.title: An untimely birth
culture.text: A stillborn child, never named, is said to be better off than a man who never enjoys life.

culture.title: A hundred children
culture.text: Many children and a proper burial were signs of a blessed life. The Preacher says neither is enough without contentment.

Ecclesiastes 7.audience: This chapter is a collection of proverbs comparing what is "better"—a good name, mourning, patience, and wisdom.

culture.title: The house of mourning
culture.text: Mourning lasted for days, with family and friends gathered. Visiting a house of mourning reminds the living of their end.

culture.title: Thorns under a pot
culture.text: Thorns burn quickly with a loud crackle but give little heat—like the laughter of fools.

Ecclesiastes 8.audience: The Preacher advises obeying the king, "in regard of the oath of God" (Ecclesiastes 8:2), and admits he cannot understand all that God does.

culture.title: The king's word
culture.text: "Where the word of a king is, there is power: and who may say unto him, What doest thou?" Royal decrees had absolute authority.

culture.title: No discharge in war
culture.text: Soldiers in battle could not leave their post. So no one can escape the day of death.

Ecclesiastes 9.audience: The Preacher urges enjoying life with one's wife and work, since the same fate comes to all.

culture.title: White garments and oil
culture.text: White garments and anointed heads were signs of celebration, the opposite of mourning in sackcloth and ashes.

culture.title: A poor wise man saves a city
culture.text: A great king besieges a small city with bulwarks (siege works), and a poor wise man delivers it but is forgotten.

Ecclesiastes 10.audience: This chapter collects proverbs on folly, rulers, and everyday dangers of work.

culture.title: Dead flies in ointment
culture.text: Perfumed oil was costly. A few dead flies could spoil a whole jar.

culture.title: Dangers of labor
culture.text: Digging a pit, breaking through a hedge (a stone wall), quarrying stones, and splitting wood could all lead to injury.

culture.title: Servants on horses
culture.text: Riding a horse was a sign of rank. Servants riding while princes walk shows the world turned upside down.

Ecclesiastes 11.audience: The Preacher urges generosity and diligence in the face of uncertainty, and calls the young to enjoy life while remembering judgment.

culture.title: Bread upon the waters
culture.text: "Cast thy bread upon the waters" may refer to sea trade or to sowing seed in wet ground—an investment whose return comes later.

culture.title: Watching the wind and clouds
culture.text: Farmers watched the weather for sowing and reaping; waiting for perfect conditions means never working.

Ecclesiastes 12.audience: The book ends with a poem on old age and death and the conclusion: "Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man" (Ecclesiastes 12:13).

culture.title: Images of old age
culture.text: Trembling keepers, few grinders, and darkened windows are often read as trembling hands, lost teeth, and failing eyes.

culture.title: The silver cord and golden bowl
culture.text: A golden lamp bowl hung by a silver cord, and a pitcher at the well—broken objects picture the end of life.

culture.title: Goads and nails
culture.text: Goads prodded oxen forward; nails fixed things firmly. Words of the wise both drive and hold.

Song of Solomon 1.audience: The book is titled "The song of songs, which is Solomon's" (Song of Solomon 1:1), a Hebrew way of saying the greatest song. It is a series of love poems between a bride and her beloved. Jewish communities read it at Passover.

culture.title: Tents of Kedar
culture.text: The Bedouin tribe of Kedar wove tents of black goat hair. The bride says she is dark from working in the sun.

culture.title: Keeping vineyards
culture.text: Young women of farming families tended vineyards outdoors, which darkened their skin.

culture.title: A bundle of myrrh
culture.text: Women wore small sachets of myrrh, a fragrant resin, on a cord around the neck.

Song of Solomon 2.audience: The beloved calls the bride to come away as winter ends: "the rain is over and gone; the flowers appear on the earth" (Song of Solomon 2:11–12).

culture.title: Spring in the land
culture.text: After the winter rains, flowers bloom, turtledoves return, figs ripen, and vines blossom—late March and April.

culture.title: Little foxes
culture.text: Foxes and jackals dug under vines and spoiled the young grapes.

culture.title: The rose of Sharon
culture.text: Sharon was the fertile coastal plain known for wildflowers. The "rose" was probably a crocus or similar bulb flower.

Song of Solomon 3.audience: The chapter describes the bride searching the city at night and Solomon's wedding procession from the wilderness.

culture.title: Watchmen in the city
culture.text: Night watchmen patrolled the city streets and walls.

culture.title: Solomon's litter
culture.text: A royal litter or palanquin, guarded by sixty mighty men, was made of cedar of Lebanon with silver, gold, and purple.

culture.title: Crowned on his wedding day
culture.text: Solomon wears the crown his mother put on him "in the day of his espousals"—grooms wore crowns or garlands at weddings.

Song of Solomon 4.audience: The beloved praises his bride in a series of images from the land—flocks, towers, and gardens—and calls her "my spouse" (Song of Solomon 4:8).

culture.title: Comparisons from the land
culture.text: Hair like goats descending Mount Gilead, teeth like freshly washed sheep, a neck like David's tower hung with shields—ancient love poetry praised beauty with images from nature and architecture.

culture.title: A garden enclosed
culture.text: Walled gardens with private springs were kept closed to strangers—an image of the bride's purity.

culture.title: Spices
culture.text: Spikenard, saffron, calamus, cinnamon, frankincense, myrrh, and aloes were costly spices, many imported from India and Arabia.

Song of Solomon 5.audience: The bride hesitates to open the door at night, then searches for her beloved and describes him to the daughters of Jerusalem.

culture.title: Feet washed for bed
culture.text: People washed their feet before bed. Getting up again meant dirtying them on the floor.

culture.title: Hand through the hole of the door
culture.text: Doors were locked by a wooden bolt reached through a hole in the door.

culture.title: Gold, ivory, and marble
culture.text: The bride describes her beloved like a costly statue of gold, ivory, sapphires, and marble.

Song of Solomon 6.audience: The bride says her beloved has gone down to his garden. He praises her again as "terrible as an army with banners" (Song of Solomon 6:4).

culture.title: Tirzah and Jerusalem
culture.text: Tirzah was a beautiful city, later the first capital of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 16:23). The bride is compared to it and to Jerusalem.

culture.title: Queens and concubines
culture.text: Royal harems included queens and concubines; the bride is called unique among them.

Song of Solomon 7.audience: The beloved praises the Shulamite from her feet to her head (Song of Solomon 7:1–9).

culture.title: Pools of Heshbon
culture.text: Heshbon, east of the Jordan, had large reservoirs; her eyes are compared to its fishpools.

culture.title: Mandrakes
culture.text: Mandrakes have a fragrant fruit and were believed to promote love and fertility (Genesis 30:14).

Song of Solomon 8.audience: The book ends with the claim that "love is strong as death" and cannot be bought (Song of Solomon 8:6–7).

culture.title: A seal on the heart
culture.text: A signet seal was worn on a cord around the neck or on a ring and identified its owner. The bride asks to be set as a seal on her beloved's heart.

culture.title: Silver and a wall for a sister
culture.text: Brothers took responsibility for an unmarried sister's protection and marriage arrangements (compare Genesis 24:50).

culture.title: Baalhamon's vineyard
culture.text: Solomon rented out his vineyard to keepers, each paying a thousand pieces of silver for its fruit.
